newsitem.title: CANADA: FIGURE SKATING-ELITE FIELD SET FOR CHAMPIONS SERIES FINAL.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-ELITE FIELD SET FOR CHAMPIONS SERIES FINAL.

text.p: Thirty of the world's best figure skaters are set for a unique showdown at the Champion Series Final Friday and Saturday, with $474,000 in prize money up for grabs at the Copps Coliseum.

The elite field features three of the four reigning world champions -- singles champions Todd Eldredge and Michelle Kwan of the United States, and pairs title holders Marina Eltsova and Andrei Bushkov of Russia.

Adding further luster to the competition are local favourite Elvis Stojko, the 1994 and 1995 world men's champion, 1994 Olympic gold medalist and last year's Series champion Alexei Urmanov of Russian, and a number of other world and Olympic medalists.
The top six point earners in singles, top four in pairs and top five dance couples from a series of six international meets held last autumn earned berths in the lucrative event.
"People are using this event to position themselves or re-establish themselves," said Canada's director general of figure skating David Dore.
"It's the championship before the championship," he said, referring to next month's World Championship in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Russia dominates the entry list with 10 contenders -- three each in men's and women's singles, and two teams in both the pairs and dance. The United States will field five entries, with two each from Canada and Ukraine. France and Germany each have one entrant.

Notably absent are Russia's world ice dance champions Oksana Grischuk and Evgeny Platov, who won last year's Final in Paris, and 1995 world gold medalist Lu Chen of China. Chen and Platov were sidelined early in the season by injuries which prevented them from qualifying.
The women's event should provide one of the more intriguing dramas. It will be an exclusive affair featuring only Americans and Russians.

In addition to the formidable challenge expected from the Russians, defending champion Kwan will again face fellow American Tara Lipinski. The 14-year-old Lipinski beat Kwan less than two weeks ago at the U.S. Nationals to become the youngest champion in that event's history.
"We're in a period of upsets," Dore said. "The person who does the performance at the moment is the one who wins. It piques your interest."

The men's competition will be another hotly-contested event with the contenders so evenly matched that the one who stays on his feet, nails the triple Axels and perhaps an elusive quadruple jump, is likely to take home the $50,000 winner's prize.
"The Champions Series Final is similar to the Olympics but by no means as intense," said Stojko, who is on a mission to reclaim his world crown.
"It has its own flavor because the top six guys are (here) and nobody else," Stojko said. "It's a very stressful competition. There you are. Go for it. There's no one else in the pack."
